newsitem.title: USA: White House confident on Lake, Herman nominations.
newsitem.headline: White House confident on Lake, Herman nominations.

text.p: The White House expressed confidence Friday that two embattled Cabinet nominees will be confirmed by the Senate once they are given a chance to answer questions about their past.

Senate committees have delayed confirmation hearings on Alexis Herman, Clinton's choice to head the Labour Department, and Anthony Lake, his nominee to serve as director of the CIA, until additional background investigations are completed.

Herman has been linked to an unfolding controversy over questionable use of the White House to court campaign contributors for the Democratic Party and Lake has been challenged for his role in secretly allowing Iran to ship arms to Bosnian Moslems, in violation of a U.N. embargo and official U.S. policy.

"Senators have to pursue questions that they think are legitimate," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said in downplaying the notion that the administration was concerned about the fate of the two nominees.

"We're respecting the advise and consent role of the Senate," McCurry said of the confirmation process. "Senators have raised questions that they want answered and have the right to get those answers."

"We're confident that ... in both cases they are meeting with senators and making very effective presentations and we're confident they will satisfy the concerns that are there and will ultimately be confirmed," McCurry said.
Herman was to meet on Friday with Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott to discuss questions raised about her actions as director of the White House office of public liaison.
Lott, a Mississippi Republican, has publicly said he believes Herman might have come close to violating the Hatch Act, which bars federal officials from partisan activities.

During Clinton's re-election campaign, Herman was responsible for inviting the comptroller of the currency, Eugene Ludwig, to a White House social gathering attended by Democratic Party fundraisers, top banking officials and Clinton.
Clinton admitted on Tuesday that Ludwig should not have been included in a gathering that mixed bankers and a federal regulator who exercises authority over them.

The nomination of Lake, the president's former national security adviser, has generated stiff opposition because of his admitted failure to notify Congress that the administration was turning a blind eye to the flow of Iranian arms to Bosnian Moslems in 1994 despite a U.N. arms embargo.
House Republicans have asked the Justice Department to investigate whether Lake, and other U.S. officials, lied to Congress about the policy. A spokesman said the request was being reviewed.

The Justice Department's Public Integrity Section already is investigating Lake's failure to comply immediately with a ruling by the White House legal counsel that he needed to sell some energy stocks in order to avoid a potential conflict of interest.
White House officials called the stocks matter a simple oversight. Lake also acknowledged that he made a mistake in not informing Congress of the Bosnian arms policy.

Thus far, the Senate has confirmed four of Clinton's nominees with little dissent -- Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Defence Secretary William Cohen, Housing and Urban Development Secretary Andrew Cuomo and Commerce Secretary William Daley.
